notes: Ruling DRP in 0. South Korea had no coalition partner, so coalition slot 13 holds the Economic Planning Board technocracy through which Park actually governed. KCIA placed in 7 as a power bloc (Stasi analogy). NDP in 1 (starting popularity) rather than MD's Democratic-lineage slot 3; its Kim Young-sam/Kim Dae-jung 'forties' revolt in 2. RPR in 4 (same organization as MD's NDFSK). md_sprites_for_tag is empty, so all icons are null. Islamic slots use the Korea Muslim Federation and small expatriate/convert circles.

0.name: Minju Konghwadang
0.text:
The Democratic Republican Party was founded in 1963 by Kim Jong-pil, with funds and cadres from the KCIA, to give General Park Chung-hee a civilian vehicle after the 1961 coup. It holds a commanding majority in the National Assembly, and the October 1969 referendum has cleared the way for Park's third term in 1971. With Kim Jong-pil sidelined, the party machine is run by the 'Four-Man System' of Kim Sung-kon, Kil Jae-ho, Kim Jin-man and Baek Nam-eok.

Its creed is the 'modernisation of the fatherland': export-led growth, anti-communism, the 1965 normalisation with Japan and the alliance with Washington, for which two Korean divisions fight in Vietnam. Its strength lies in the countryside, the bureaucracy and the political funds of the chaebol.

1.name: Sinmindang
1.text:
The New Democratic Party was formed in February 1967 by the merger of the Minjung Party and Yun Po-sun's New Korea Party, and inherits the conservative lineage of the Korea Democratic Party of 1945. Beaten in the 1967 elections and outmanoeuvred over the third-term amendment, it enters 1970 led by the ailing Yu Chin-o, with the veteran organiser Yu Jin-san preparing to take the chair, while the younger Kim Young-sam and Kim Dae-jung demand the 1971 presidential nomination.

The party defends parliamentary democracy, civil liberties and fair elections while remaining firmly anti-communist and pro-American. Its base is the cities, Seoul above all, the educated middle class and the opposition press.

2.name: Sasipdae Kisu
2.text:
In November 1969 Kim Young-sam, aged 41, declared that the opposition needed a standard-bearer in his forties for the 1971 presidential race, defying the party elders. Kim Dae-jung and Lee Chul-seung quickly followed with bids of their own, and the 'forties standard-bearer' slogan has become a generational revolt inside the New Democratic Party.

The young turks promise a mass opposition able to defeat Park at the ballot box: honest elections, an end to KCIA surveillance, labour rights, a fairer share for the neglected provinces and fresh ideas on reunification and détente among the great powers around the peninsula. Their leverage lies with students, young urban voters and the party's ambitious second rank.

3.name: T'ongil Sahoedang
3.text:
The Unification Socialist Party descends from the reformist socialist parties that flourished briefly after the April Revolution of 1960 and were crushed by the 1961 coup. Re-established as a tiny legal party, it is led by Kim Chul, who cultivates ties with the Socialist International and the social democratic parties of Western Europe.

It advocates a welfare state, independent trade unions, land and tax reform, and peaceful reunification through negotiation, while rejecting Pyongyang's communism. Every proposal on unification risks prosecution under the Anti-Communist Law, so the party survives on intellectuals, a handful of union activists and the goodwill of foreign socialist parties.

4.name: T'ongil Hyŏngmyŏngdang
4.text:
The Revolutionary Party for Reunification is the underground party built in South Korea under direction from Pyongyang. Its network was broken by the KCIA in August 1968 and its leader Kim Jong-tae was executed in July 1969 with other cadres, but surviving cells and the Workers' Party of Korea keep its name alive as the authentic voice of the southern revolution.

It calls for the withdrawal of American troops, the overthrow of the 'Park puppet clique' and reunification on Pyongyang's terms through a people's democratic revolution. Its following is limited to clandestine cells of students, intellectuals and former members of the southern Workers' Party, yet every arrest feeds the regime's anti-communist propaganda.

5.name: Yuksam Sedae
5.text:
The June Third Generation are the student militants forged in the protests of 3 June 1964 against normalisation with Japan, when martial law was declared in Seoul. Expelled, drafted or jailed, leaders such as Kim Jung-tae passed the torch to the campuses that fought the third-term amendment in 1969, and underground study circles at Seoul National and Korea University keep the tradition alive.

They denounce dependence on Japanese and American capital, military rule and the KCIA, and demand self-reliant nationalism, social justice and genuine democracy. Their leverage is the campus: the universities can be mobilised within days, and a student uprising has already toppled one president in April 1960.

6.name: Sŏnggyun'gwan
6.text:
Sungkyunkwan, the royal Confucian academy and shrine of the Chosŏn dynasty in Seoul, remains the national headquarters of Korean Confucianism, presiding over the local hyanggyo schools and the great lineage associations. Its elders carry the authority of the old yangban clans and lead the rites to Confucius held each spring and autumn.

They reject Western individualism, Christian proselytising and mass culture as corrosive, and defend the patriarchal family law, including the ban on marriage between people of the same surname and ancestral seat, against the women's organisations campaigning for reform. Anti-communist but suspicious of American influence, they draw their leverage from ancestral villages, clan networks and the conscience of the older generation.

7.name: Chungang Chŏngbobu
7.text:
The Korean Central Intelligence Agency was created by Kim Jong-pil in June 1961, weeks after the coup, and has grown into the regime's political nerve centre. After the long tenure of Kim Hyong-uk, who staged the 1967 East Berlin spy affair and drove the third-term campaign, it passed in October 1969 to the former army chief of staff Kim Kye-won.

The agency spies on opposition politicians, students, journalists and Koreans abroad, drafts election strategy, funds the ruling party and runs covert operations against the North. It answers to Park alone and stands above the law: whoever controls its files and its interrogation rooms on Namsan holds the most dangerous lever in Korean politics.

8.name: Hey'at-e Seul
8.text:
The Seoul Muharram Circle is a small gathering of Iranian merchants, students and visiting engineers who meet in private homes in Seoul to mourn Imam Husayn during Muharram and to hold Friday readings. With no mosque of their own, they occasionally pray alongside the Sunni converts of the Korea Muslim Federation.

Its members read the modernist sermons of Morteza Motahhari and the lectures of Tehran's Hosseiniyeh Ershad, which present Shia Islam as a faith of reason, social justice and progress. They have no political weight in Korea, but act as an informal bridge for trade and cultural contacts between Seoul and Tehran.

9.name: Maktab-e Najaf
9.text:
The Najaf Circle is a tiny knot of devout Iranian students and traders in Korea who follow Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled by the Shah in 1964 and now teaching in Najaf. They pay their religious dues to his representatives, pass around his treatises and letters smuggled out of Iraq, and keep their distance from the Shah's officials.

They hold that the Pahlavi monarchy is illegitimate, that Iran is being sold to America and Israel, and that the religious jurists must guide the Muslim community. In Seoul they are politically invisible, yet they link a few Korean converts to the Najaf networks that dream of overthrowing the Shah.

10.name: Han'guk Isŭllamgyo Chunganghoe
10.text:
The Korea Muslim Federation was organised in 1967 out of the Korea Islamic Society, founded in 1955 by Koreans converted by the imams of the Turkish Brigade during the Korean War. It represents a community of a few thousand believers, still worshipping in a makeshift prayer hall in Seoul while it seeks land and foreign funds for a proper central mosque.

The federation is loyal to the government and fiercely anti-communist, cultivating Saudi Arabia, Malaysia and the Muslim World League as patrons and offering Seoul a channel to the oil-rich Arab world. Its influence rests on these foreign sponsors and on official recognition, not on numbers.

11.name: Halaqat al-Khilafa
11.text:
The Caliphate Study Circle is a handful of Arab and Pakistani students and a few young Korean converts who meet in Seoul to read the pamphlets of Hizb ut-Tahrir and the prison writings of Sayyid Qutb, hanged in Cairo in 1966. They have no organisation beyond their study evenings and their correspondence with brethren abroad.

They reject nation-states, monarchies and the Korea Muslim Federation's deference to the government alike, and teach that only a restored caliphate under Islamic law can unite the umma against both American capitalism and Soviet atheism. Their reach is negligible, but they offer an uncompromising creed to converts disillusioned with official Islam.

12.name: Usrat Seoul
12.text:
The Seoul Usra is a Muslim Brotherhood 'family' cell formed by Egyptian, Jordanian and Syrian students and technicians in South Korea, together with Korean converts eager for religious instruction. It meets weekly for Qur'an study and mutual aid, following the method of Hassan al-Banna.

The usra preaches gradual Islamic renewal through education, charity and missionary work, accepting lawful government while insisting that Muslims organise and be heard. It wants the Korea Muslim Federation to grow from a diplomatic showcase into a preaching movement, and it draws on literature and contacts from Said Ramadan's Islamic Centre in Geneva.

13.name: Kyŏngje Kihoegwŏn
13.text:
The Economic Planning Board was created by the military government in 1961 as a super-ministry commanding the budget, foreign loans and the five-year plans, and its minister ranks as Deputy Prime Minister. Since June 1969 it has been led by Kim Hak-ryul, while the economist Kim Chung-yum became Park's chief secretary in October 1969, putting technocrats at the heart of the Blue House.

The planners stand for growth above politics: export targets, cheap credit to favoured firms, foreign capital, the Seoul-Pusan expressway and heavy industry such as the planned steelworks at Pohang. Loyal to Park rather than to the party, they draw their leverage from allocating every loan, licence and import quota in the country.

14.name: Nongŏp Hyŏptong Chohap Chunganghoe
14.text:
The National Agricultural Cooperative Federation was formed in 1961 when the junta merged the agricultural bank and the village co-operatives into a single state-supervised network. Its president is appointed by the government, and it reaches nearly every farming household through township co-operatives that distribute fertiliser, credit and seed.

Its constituency is the conservative, deferential countryside where half of all Koreans still live and where the ruling party wins its majorities. The federation champions rural credit, rice price support and village improvement, while resenting the drain of young people and capital to the cities. Whoever controls its fertiliser and loans controls the rural vote.

15.name: Chŏn'guk Kyŏngjein Yŏnhaphoe
15.text:
The Federation of Korean Industries began in 1961 as the Korean Businessmen's Association, founded by Samsung's Lee Byung-chul after the junta threatened leading entrepreneurs with prosecution for illicit wealth. Renamed in 1968 and chaired by the textile magnate Kim Yong-wan, it gathers the heads of the rising chaebol, from Samsung to Chung Ju-yung's Hyundai.

Its members trade loyalty and political funds for state-guaranteed loans, licences and export subsidies. They favour cheap labour, weak unions and close ties with Japanese capital, and they quietly finance the ruling party. Their leverage is simple: Park's growth plan cannot work without them.

16.name: Chungso Kiŏp Hyŏptong Chohap Chunganghoe
16.text:
The Korea Federation of Small Business was founded in 1962 to group the co-operatives of the small and medium firms that make up the great majority of Korean enterprises, from Seoul's garment workshops to provincial foundries. It operates under government supervision, but its members increasingly complain of being squeezed by the favoured conglomerates.

The federation calls for fair access to bank credit, an end to collusive licensing, lower taxes and less bureaucratic interference, arguing that competition rather than state favour should drive growth. Politically cautious and anti-communist, it draws its leverage from the shopkeepers, subcontractors and artisans who resent the privileges of the chaebol.

17.name: Han'guk Chayŏn Pojŏn Hyŏphoe
17.english: Korean Association for Conservation of Nature
17.text:
The Korean Association for Conservation of Nature grew out of a circle of biologists and foresters formed in the early 1960s to survey the peninsula's surviving wildlife and forests after decades of war and fuel-wood cutting. It welcomed the designation of Chirisan as the country's first national park in December 1967, won after a campaign by local residents.

It argues for reforestation of the bare hills, protected mountains and wetlands, and controls on the pollution beginning to spread from new industrial zones such as Ulsan. Its members are academics, foresters and teachers with little political weight, but reforestation is a cause even the regime embraces.

18.name: Tosi Sanŏp Sŏn'gyohoe
18.text:
The Urban Industrial Mission is the labour ministry of Korea's Presbyterian and Methodist churches, begun in 1958 and renamed from 'industrial evangelism' in the late 1960s as its pastors moved from preaching in factories to organising workers. Its centres in Yŏngdŭngp'o and Inch'ŏn are run by figures such as the American missionary George Ogle and the Methodist pastor Cho Wha-soon.

It teaches workers their rights under the labour law, trains shop-floor leaders and helps build independent unions, especially among young women in textile and electronics plants. It rejects Marxism but condemns the exploitation behind the export drive, and its leverage lies in church protection and international ecumenical networks.

19.name: Inmin Hyŏngmyŏngdang
19.text:
The People's Revolutionary Party is an underground network of Taegu-based socialists, teachers and veterans of the reformist parties of 1960. Exposed by the KCIA in August 1964, when leaders including Do Ye-jong were tried and imprisoned, it has since regrouped quietly in study circles in the southeastern cities.

It seeks an independent Korean socialism: neutral reunification free of both Washington and Moscow, land and labour reform, and a democratic people's government rather than Pyongyang's personality cult. Its leverage is small but persistent, rooted in the radical traditions of the Kyŏngsang provinces and in a new generation of students.

20.name: Han'guk Pan'gong Yŏnmaeng
20.text:
The Korean Anti-Communist League was established by law in 1964 as the successor to the Korean chapter of the Asian People's Anti-Communist League, founded under Syngman Rhee and Chiang Kai-shek in 1954. Funded by the state, it runs rallies, lectures and propaganda drives and keeps close ties with anti-communist movements across Asia.

It mobilises veterans, refugees from the North, Christian anti-communists and patriotic youth against 'impure elements', and after the 1968 Blue House raid and the Pueblo seizure it demands harsher punishment of leftists and a harder line toward Pyongyang. Its leverage lies in the mass rally and in branding any critic a fellow traveller.

21.name: Ilminjuŭi
21.text:
Ilminjuŭi, the 'One-People Principle', was the official doctrine of Syngman Rhee's early republic, devised by the philosopher Ahn Ho-sang and spread through Lee Beom-seok's Korean National Youth Association, modelled on the Hitler Youth and the Chinese Blue Shirts. Long out of power, its veterans gather around Ahn and the ageing Lee, nursing the dream of a disciplined national community.

The doctrine proclaims one race, one bloodline and one will, subordinating class, region and party to the nation under a strong leader. Its followers want a militarised youth movement, total anti-communist mobilisation and national purification from foreign decadence, and they find willing listeners among officers and anti-communist youth leagues.

22.name: Taehan Min'guk Yukkun
22.text:
The Republic of Korea Army, over half a million strong, is the backbone of Park Chung-hee's state and the institution that brought him to power in May 1961. Two of its divisions, the Tiger and the White Horse, fight in South Vietnam, and since the commando raid on the Blue House in January 1968 it has stood on permanent alert along the DMZ.

The officer corps, led by graduates of the Korean Military Academy, sees itself as the guardian of the nation against communism and civilian disorder. Within it the secret Hanahoe club of young officers such as Chun Doo-hwan and Roh Tae-woo is building loyalty to Park and to one another, a reserve of power should the President falter.

23.name: Yi Wangga
23.text:
The House of Yi ruled Korea for over five centuries until the Japanese annexation of 1910. Its head, Crown Prince Yi Un, returned from Japan in 1963 after decades of exile and now lies gravely ill at Nakseonjae in Changdeok Palace, attended by his Japanese-born wife Yi Bang-ja; his son Yi Ku, an architect trained in America, is the heir.

The family has no political role and depends on a modest state allowance. Monarchist sentiment survives among elders of the Chŏnju Yi lineage and Confucian traditionalists who see the dynasty as a symbol of national dignity and continuity, untainted by the quarrels of the republic.
